articles.title: FBI, Georgia officials arrest suspect in New York for death threat against Collins, son-in-law
articles.summary: The FBI and Georgia law enforcement officials have arrested a suspect in New York who allegedly threatened Georgia Senate GOP candidate Mike Collins and his son-in-law, they announced Monday. The FBI said on X that the agency, the Georgia Bureau of Investigation and the Butts County Sheriff’s Office had arrested a suspect in Buffalo, N.Y.,…
articles.body:
The FBI and Georgia law enforcement officials have arrested a suspect in New York who allegedly threatened Georgia Senate GOP candidate Mike Collins and his son-in-law, they announced Monday.

The FBI said on X that the agency, the Georgia Bureau of Investigation and the Butts County Sheriff’s Office had arrested a suspect in Buffalo, N.Y., accused of making a death threat against the congressman and his son-in-law.

The Butts County Sheriff’s Office identified the suspect as Anthony Lantrell Bennett of Buffalo and said in a post on Facebook that he had been arrested and charged with two counts of terroristic threats on Friday.

The suspect acknowledged that he had threatened both men, and officials “determined the threat was connected to information in an online story that was not accurate or true,” according to the sheriff’s office.

“State lines don’t protect those who threaten violence, and they do not stop the FBI and our law enforcement partners from pursuing them,” FBI Buffalo Special Agent-in-Charge Allen D. Davis II said in a statement. “Strong law enforcement partnerships are critical to our mission.”

Collins, in a statement on X , thanked law enforcement, saying he was “grateful to the FBI, the Butts County Sheriff’s Department, and all law enforcement partners for acting quickly to protect my family.”

The Georgia Senate GOP candidate suggested that his opponent, Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), bore some responsibility for the incident.

“It’s become fashionable for leftist to say anything they want about their Republican opponents to try to irrationally and inaccurately paint them as monsters,” Collins wrote. “My opponent clearly likes to play that irresponsible game, and here we are. When you mix false accusations with inflammatory rhetoric, it fuels the lunatics who want to settle political disagreements with violence.”

Collins called on Ossoff to condemn political violence, adding that the senator “should apologize, retract his false attacks, and campaign on the issues affecting Georgians.”

When reached for comment, an Ossoff campaign spokesperson said, “Senator Ossoff condemns all threats of violence.” Ossoff’s team has not told NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network, whether the two men have spoken since the incident.

Collins is vying to oust Ossoff in the Senate this fall, though a polling average of Georgia Senate surveys compiled by Decision Desk HQ shows Ossoff holding a 9-point lead.

Collins has faced growing scrutiny as several of his former aides and relatives have been embroiled in controversy, including his son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, whom CNN’s KFile reported in July has previously shared antisemitic and white nationalist rhetoric.

“He doesn’t speak for me. I don’t speak for him. No one speaks for me, and I don’t speak for anyone else,” Collins told reporters in August when asked about his son-in-law. “I condemn all forms of anti-Semitism. I don’t care what the source is.”

There has been a troubling uptick in political violence in recent years, including President Trump’s near assassination in Pennsylvania in 2024, conservative Charlie Kirk’s assassination in 2025 and the murder of a Minnesota state lawmaker in 2025.

NewsNation’s Ava Thompson contributed to this report.

He warned in the letter that his district is a "suspected hotspot of this fraud" and offered himself as "an interlocutor to help enable cooperation with state-level agencies and law enforcement." Georgia's 7th Congressional District, which McCormick represents, encompasses part of the Atlanta metro area including the city's northern suburbs. articles.title: Sununu rattles off disagreements with Trump at New Hampshire town hall
articles.summary: Former Sen. John Sununu (R-N.H.) rattled off his many disagreements with President Trump at a New Hampshire town hall ahead of the November midterm elections, when he’ll face Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.). In particular, Sununu criticized the president’s war in Iran and trade conflict with Canada. When asked if he would be a Republican dissenter…
articles.body:
Former Sen. John Sununu (R-N.H.) rattled off his many disagreements with President Trump at a New Hampshire town hall ahead of the November midterm elections, when he’ll face Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.).

In particular, Sununu criticized the president’s war in Iran and trade conflict with Canada.

When asked if he would be a Republican dissenter against some of Trump’s policies, the former senator said, “You can just start by looking at what I’ve been saying consistently for the last 10 months, we shouldn’t be in a trade war with Canada.”

“I said earlier we shouldn’t have tariffs on building materials. I said it was a mistake to go into Iran without a fixed proposal and plan for keeping the Strait of Hormuz open,” he continued. “I opposed the $5,000 one-time payments that were recently proposed, the $1.8 billion victims fund. So, this has never been an issue for me, because I believe all of those positions sort of reflect the thinking of most of the people in New Hampshire.”

Sununu cited past examples of his break from the Republican party including his opposition against the Patriot Act in 2005 alongside only 5 other Republican senators.

“And if you look back at the issues we raised about these surveillance powers [in the Patriot Act], we were right. They were misused by Republican presidents and Democrat presidents,” he concluded.

Sununu joins other GOP candidates in battleground elections who have distanced themselves from Trump , particularly about the ongoing Iran war . Iowa Senate candidate Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) and Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Rep. Tom Tiffany (R-Wis.), for example, both called for an end to the conflict earlier this year.

Trump’s popularity in the Granite State also hit an all-time low in September, according to a University of New Hampshire poll , which found 67 percent of respondents disapproved of Trump’s overall job as president. Thirty-two percent approved and 1 percent were unsure.

Sununu is currently trailing Pappas by 5-points, receiving 45 percent backing compared to 50 percent support earned by his Democratic opponent, according to New York Times/Siena polling released in September.

New Hampshire is neither a solidly blue nor red state with its state Legislature flipping between Democratic and Republican control in recent years. It is now led by a Republican , Gov. Kelly Ayotte.

articles.title: Trump turns to emerging tech giant in multi-billion bid to ramp up US submarine production
articles.summary: Silicon Valley giant Anduril plans to invest $3.7 billion building a massive Baltimore shipyard to break Virginia-class submarine bottlenecks.
articles.body: The Trump administration is turning to a defense technology giant in a $6.6 billion effort to speed production of submarines as the U.S. struggles to keep pace with China's vast shipbuilding capacity. The ramp-up in production brings a Silicon Valley-style manufacturer into one of the Pentagon's most troubled industrial bases as they fall behind expected pace of two Virginia-class attack submarines per year. Anduril will build a more than 2-million-square-foot shipyard at Sparrows Point shipyard just outside of Baltimore to manufacture critical submarine components, eventually scaling up to large sections of the vessels. A senior administration official said the facility could add roughly 9 million labor hours a year, equivalent to about a 15% increase in submarine production capacity. President Donald Trump will visit the shipyard on Tuesday afternoon to formally announce the new initiative in Baltimore alongside Anduril leadership. NAVY SECRETARY WARNS SHIPYARDS MUST ‘ACT LIKE WE’RE AT WAR’ AS CHINA’S AI-POWERED FLEET RACES AHEAD The investment takes aim at a problem the Navy has struggled for years to solve: shipyards are delivering roughly 1.3 Virginia-class submarines a year, well short of the Navy's goal of two, even as demand for the nuclear-powered attack boats grows. The Navy currently projects reaching the two-per-year rate around 2032. It currently has 26 Virginia-class submarines and expects to add two more in the spring, according to a senior administration official.and For the submarine project, Anduril plans to invest $3.7 billion of its own capital to build the facility, workforce and manufacturing capacity. The Navy could spend up to another $2.9 billion purchasing the resulting production. The deal represents an unusual bet on a commercial model for fixing one of the Pentagon's most stubborn industrial problems: Anduril will risk billions of dollars of its own capital building new submarine production capacity, while the Navy pays for what the company can successfully produce. "I wouldn't say that the government's paying us back. We feel the government [is] buying the results of what we're able to produce," an industry official told reporters of the deal. EMERGING TECH HAS NEW ARMY LEADERS WARNING TROOPS CAN'T ‘AI’ THEIR WAY TO VICTORY ON THE BATTLEFIELD The deal also deepens Anduril's growing relationship with the Pentagon just days after War Secretary Pete Hegseth tapped company founder Palmer Luckey, along with Elon Musk and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich, to launch Project Meridian — a 120-day study of how future wars will be fought and what weapons and technologies the U.S. military will need. The arrangement puts Luckey in a position to help shape recommendations about the Pentagon's future technology needs as the company he founded expands its own business selling weapons and other systems to the department. Project Meridian does not have procurement authority, and the Pentagon has said "appropriate" safeguards will be used to address potential conflicts of interest. Anduril will work under General Dynamics Electric Boat and alongside HII's Newport News Shipbuilding, initially producing components that have become bottlenecks in the construction of new Virginia-class boats. Among the first will be torpedo tubes , which a senior administration official described as a current "gating component" holding up production. The official said getting those tubes earlier could allow the Navy to move. Anduril has already begun work on torpedo tubes at a facility in California and plans to shift that production to Baltimore as the new shipyard, dubbed Arsenal-2, comes online. The company eventually hopes to move from individual components to complex modules and large sections of submarines. "We just need new production capacity," an industry official said. "We need to grow the maritime industrial base, the submarine industrial base, so that we can produce more submarines." The company plans to build Arsenal-2 around software, automation and digital manufacturing to break historically complex shipbuilding work into simpler tasks that can be done without years of shipyard experience. The push comes as the Navy faces growing pressure to expand the attack-submarine fleet while also preparing to transfer Virginia-class submarines to Australia under the AUKUS security pact. Meeting those commitments will require the industrial base not only to reach the Navy's longstanding two-per-year goal, but eventually move beyond it. Arsenal-2 is expected to create 3,100 direct jobs and another 11,000 indirect jobs nationwide. Anduril expects the Baltimore facility to begin operations around 2030, though the company said production of some submarine components is beginning now in California. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The approach will still have to clear the certification and safety requirements that govern nuclear submarine construction. Anduril acknowledged that it will have to prove it can meet those standards before graduating from individual components to increasingly complex sections of the boats.

articles.title: Congress has never passed a real budget
articles.summary: Author Kurt Couchman argues that Congress must move beyond temporary funding extensions and implement a comprehensive annual budget process that integrates both spending and revenue to regain fiscal control and restore public trust.
articles.body:
Fiscal 2026 ended on Sept. 30. Congress has avoided a shutdown — again — by extending current funding through Dec. 11.

But merely keeping the lights on is a pathetic measure of successful budgeting. Not one of the 12 appropriations bills has been enacted, and the Senate Appropriations Committee still hasn’t released its versions.

In fact, Congress has never done a real budget. A real budget would be one bill that covers all spending and revenue, managed through committees that are supposed to be responsible for updating, coordinating, and otherwise overseeing those programs.

The 12 appropriations bills cover only one-fourth of spending and no revenue. They involve just one committee and a sliver of members in each house.

The budget resolution should be the blueprint to guide and start the yearly congressional budget process. Instead, it has become merely a vessel for occasional fast-track budget reconciliation when one party controls the House, the Senate and the presidency.

That’s why appropriations bills struggle every year. Most members have little stake in the product, so they have little reason to fight for bills they didn’t help write. The result: Appropriations arrive late, get punted into stopgaps, and rarely change much from year to year.

As a share of the economy and as a share of the budget, annual appropriations have shrunk for decades — this “discretionary” spending fell from 9.7 percent of GDP in 1986 to 6.2 percent in 2025.

Yet spending on autopilot has grown much faster than revenue. Direct spending, net of user fees, grew from 9.2 percent of GDP to 13.7 percent over the same stretch — while revenue barely moved, averaging 17.2 percent of GDP over the last 40 years, just 0.2 percentage points above 1986 collections.

Congress’s grip on the budget is exceptionally weak today. It can’t actively manage most spending, and what little comes up each year is so tightly controlled it largely runs on autopilot, too. That’s why borrowing keeps growing, and why Americans are stuck with higher inflation, higher interest rates, and slower growth.

The fix is simple: Congress should build a real budget every year. Real budgeting is exactly what businesses do all the time — look at revenue and expenses together, not as separate conversations. That means one bill covering all spending and revenue, managed by the committees that oversee each program, with every representative and senator able to weigh in.

All committees would do what appropriators do each year — review and adjust their programs — with oversight from the Budget Committees.

Comprehensive budgeting would give Congress far more control over the policies that drive borrowing — and, by extension, over the inflation, interest rates, and slower growth that come with it. It would also mean better stewardship of taxpayer funds, including catching waste, fraud and abuse that autopilot spending currently obscures.

Most important, letting all members of Congress, not just those in the majority party, actually shape spending and revenue decisions would mean more Americans see their own priorities reflected in the budget. Congress might even earn back some of the trust it’s lost.

Holistic budget management has helped countries turn themselves around. Before 2017, Ireland considered spending and revenue separately and paid dearly for it. Government debt nearly quintupled as a share of the economy during and after the 2008 financial crisis, rising from 24 percent of GDP in 2007 to 119 percent in 2012. After Ireland began managing spending and revenue together, its economy grew so much faster than its debt that the ratio fell to just 33 percent of GDP by 2025.

Applied to Congress, a real budget process would also strengthen the ties between members, who would need each other’s votes and support to advance their priorities. A more cohesive Congress, with members invested in each other’s success, would be far better positioned to serve the people who sent them there.

Avoiding a shutdown was never the goal. Governing is. Congress won’t get there by merely surviving the next deadline. It will get there by finally building a budget worthy of the name.

Kurt Couchman is senior fellow in fiscal policy at Americans for Prosperity and author of “Fiscal Democracy in America: How a Balanced Budget Amendment Can Restore Sound Governance.”

articles.title: Trump’s California quip blows up
articles.summary: Plus: 🌮First Tuesday of October means National Taco Day! {beacon} It’s Tuesday. Looking for something good to watch tonight? There are plenty of midterm debates to tune into. We’ll fill you in. In today’s issue: Trump’s California comments Collins and Jackson debate in Maine Firing squad for convicted terrorist WHO update on Russia plague…
articles.body:
It’s Tuesday. Looking for something good to watch tonight? There are plenty of midterm debates to tune into. We’ll fill you in.

Programming note : We’re Joshua Feldstein and Claire Leibowitz, filling in for Cate today. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to jfeldstein@thehill.com or cleibowitz@thehill.com .

The Associated Press | Charlie Riedel and Jae C. Hong

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) called President Trump “deranged and dangerous” following his comments on Monday that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego.

“It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, for keeping our country safe,” Trump said at a Monday rally in Grand Island, Neb. “Let ’em take out Los Angeles, let ’em take out San Diego.”

“After sending the National Guard to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego,” Newsom wrote on social media . “He is deranged and dangerous.”

The White House pushed back on California officials’ response to Trump’s comments, with communications director Steven Cheung saying, “The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality.”

“He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped. America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money,” Cheung wrote on social media.

Encouraging attacks: Newsom and other California politicians believe the president was encouraging violence on their state.

“At least 19 servicemembers have made the ultimate sacrifice in Trump’s unauthorized war with Iran — including Noah Tietjens of Nebraska,” Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) wrote on the social platform X about Trump’s comments in Nebraska.

“Now Trump is in Nebraska inviting an attack on U.S. soil, putting millions of Americans and hundreds of thousands of our servicemembers at risk while trying to get Americans to cheer for an attack on our own country,” Padilla continued. “What kind of Commander in Chief does that?”

Los Angeles’s Mayor Karen Bass (D) wrote on the social platform X that Trump’s comments “are dangerous and could potentially compromise our safety.”

“The role of the president is to protect the country, not actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives,” Bass continued.

San Diego’s mayor Todd Gloria (D) also told the president to “keep our city out of your reckless war talk,” in a social media post .

FBI warned California in February: Multiple outlets reported on March 11 that the FBI warned California police departments of potential retaliatory Iranian attacks on California’s coastline.

The agency’s Joint Terrorism Task Force reportedly sent memos to police departments across the Golden State in late February that Iran allegedly “aspired to conduct a surprise attack” on the state’s coastal cities.

On March 12, the day after the FBI report came out, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt pushed back on the FBI’s attack claims, saying there was “no such threat from Iran to our homeland.”

Trump told reporters at the time that he was not worried about retaliatory strikes on the U.S., according to Reuters.

➤ TRUMP SPURS ANTI-TRANS BLOWBACK IN SC:

President Trump’s anti-trans comments made towards South Carolina Senate candidate Annie Andrews (D), a cisgender mother of three, have stirred up some controversy among Democratic and GOP lawmakers.

“Annie ‘T——’ Andrews is running against our wonderful Darline Graham [R-S.C.] for the Senate in South Carolina,” the president wrote on Truth Social, later repeating the slur.

Andrews stays on message: Andrews responded saying she’s “going to work with anyone to put South Carolina first, because lowering costs and making life better for families across our state is going to take all of us working together.”

Former South Carolina Gov. David Beasley (R), who was in office from 1995 to 1999, chimed in on the social platform X, calling Trump’s comments “abhorrent.”

“South Carolina deserves better,” Beasley continued. “I urge voters to look at the merits of each candidate and cast their vote accordingly. We must reject politics based on division and hate.”

According to current predictions from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), Graham has a 72 percent chance of winning.

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and former state Senate President Troy Jackson are set to face off in their first debate Tuesday night at 7 p.m. EDT.

Jackson got the Democratic nod after Graham Platner dropped out of his campaign in July over allegations of rape, which he denied.

Jackson largely picked up where Platner left off, trying to tie Collins to President Trump in the blue state.

On this day 8 years ago… Collins voted to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh. Democrats have tried to dig into this point , as the justice became a deciding vote to overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022. Collins has said she doesn’t regret support Kavanaugh, but disagrees with his decision in the landmark case.

Jackson is lesser known around the state, so the five debates planned with Collins will be a high-stakes opportunity to make an impression — for better or worse.

Jackson has held 50 public events and participated in 67 interviews in the 10 weeks since he became nominee, NBC reports .

Tight fight: DDHQ currently forecasts that Jackson holds a slight edge over Collins. But the two have been going back and forth.

Collins and Jackson are set to debate again Thursday night.

State auditor and Democrat Rob Sand has been leading his GOP opponent Zach Lahn in polls for months. Tonight, they will debate at 8 p.m. EDT.

At stake on stage: Tonight’s questions will be focused on the economy and cost of living, according to KWQC , the debate’s host.

Republicans in rural areas have been struggling to put forward a positive message on affordability as the war in Iran drives up energy prices and fuels broader inflation.

The GOP nominee for Senate, Rep. Ashley Hinson , has broken with Trump, calling to end the war and impose a diesel export ban. Lahn has largely stuck with the president.

Sand and Lahn are fighting to succeed Gov. Kim Reynolds’s (R), one of the least popular governors in the country.

Michigan politics watchers are in for a busy week: Candidates face off in a gubernatorial debate Tuesday, the state’s 7th Congressional District Wednesday, and then former Rep. Mike Rogers (R) and his Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed meet for the first Senate debate on Thursday.

Tuesday’s 7 p.m. EDT match-up is between Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and Republican Congressman John James , who has been endorsed by Trump.

According to DDHQ, Benson is slightly favored to replace Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D), who is term limited.

Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced Monday that convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan, who opened fire on U.S. troops at Ft. Hood in 2009, will be sentenced to death by firing squad.

“The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution,” Parnell said. “Judgement day for Hasan has finally come.”

What happened at Ft. Hood?: Hasan opened fire at a medical facility at Ft. Hood on Nov. 5, 2009, killing 13 people and injuring 32 others.

During the attack, he continuously shouted “Allahu Akbar.”

How often is the firing squad done?: The last person to be executed by firing squad in the United States was 67-year-old Brad Sigmon in 2025.

Sigmon was convicted in South Carolina of killing his ex-girlfriend’s parents in 2001 and was sentenced to death in 2002. Before Sigmon, nobody had been killed by firing squad in 15 years.

The last death sentence carried out by the U.S. military was in 1961.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a statewide measles emergency Monday. The state has reported 108 measles cases as of Oct. 3, state officials have reported.

Paramount closed a multi-billion-dollar deal to acquire Warner Brothers Discovery on Tuesday, which will create the largest provider of news, sports and entertainment.

The World Health Organization (WHO) said no further signs of infection have been detected at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia. Authorities are still investigating if the pneumonic plague caused a researcher’s death in Russia.

Cornell University faculty have prepared a no-confidence resolution against the university’s administration over their handling of the alleged gang rape in 2024. The resolution is led by Paul Ortiz , a professor of labor history at Cornell.

articles.title: A surprising industry is fueling a new rush for gold — and it’s not slowing down
articles.summary: Gold demand from AI infrastructure and semiconductors is climbing even as prices hit historic highs, and tech firms aren't switching to cheaper metals.
articles.body: Investors have long prized gold as a hedge against inflation and economic uncertainty, but one of the world’s fastest-growing industries is now fueling a new source of demand for the precious metal. The buildout of artificial intelligence (AI) is driving investment in advanced semiconductors, servers and the sprawling data centers needed to power the technology. That expansion also requires a range of materials used in high-performance electronics, including gold. And the AI boom is creating a growing need at a time when gold is already historically expensive. Despite those high prices, tech companies aren't necessarily switching to cheaper materials — suggesting demand for golf could continue to grow alongside AI. A QUIET RUSH FOR GOLD IS SWEEPING THE GLOBE — HERE'S WHY COUNTRIES ARE STOCKPILING IT Gold is valued in electronics for its conductivity, reliability and resistance to corrosion — and its role in some technology applications is proving resilient despite trading at roughly $4,153 an ounce on Oct. 5, up nearly 6%, or about $225, from a year earlier. Joseph Cavatoni, a gold market expert and senior market strategist for North America at the World Gold Council, said companies would typically consider cheaper alternatives after developing technology that relies on gold. But that isn't necessarily happening. "They might pioneer a technology with gold involved and then say, ‘Let’s find something cheaper like tungsten to replace it,’" Cavatoni told Fox News Digital. "But what we’re finding in this case is they’re not." ONE OF THE WORLD'S HOTTEST INDUSTRIES IS SPARKING A BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM Technology demand is already showing signs of growth. Gold demand from the sector rose 2% from a year earlier to 80.4 metric tons in the second quarter, according to the World Gold Council. Electronics demand climbed 4% to 68.3 tons, fueled by AI infrastructure, high-end semiconductors and advanced components. Cavatoni said gold can offer advantages over substitutes in applications such as chip production and heat conduction. The AI sector may also be less sensitive to elevated gold prices because relatively small amounts of the metal are needed. "This is a rapidly growing space that’s less sensitive to price," Cavatoni said. "It’s going to likely continue to grow as the AI space grows." Cavatoni said it is "less likely to be a driver of the price of gold." For now, Cavatoni described technology as an increasingly important contributor to gold demand that "doesn’t appear to be slowing down anytime soon."

articles.title: Republicans sound alarm over hidden midterm stakes that could reshape Supreme Court for decades
articles.summary: Sen. Steve Daines warns that losing the Senate could block Trump's Supreme Court nominees, urging disgruntled Republicans to rally behind candidates.
articles.body: Republicans are quietly warning that the true consequence of losing the Senate could be one that shapes the makeup of courts and the law for years to come. While Republican candidates and surrogates on the campaign trail are warning of a rise in socialism and a return to Biden-era policy should Democrats flip Congress this cycle, some are pushing a different message: if Democrats win the Senate, they’ll block future Supreme Court nominees. "I think the key over the next 34 days is bringing home Republicans. And I think it's important to remind some of these Republicans who are not energized yet that the Supreme Court's on the ballot," Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., told Fox News Digital. BATTLE OVER DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME ERUPTS AS PUSH TO STOP CHANGING CLOCKS HITS SENATE WALL Daines, who chaired the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) in 2024, played a key role in flipping the Senate two years ago. That election was dominated by pocketbook issues, much like this midterm cycle, and Democrats have pounced upon that message. But the Supreme Court and the implications of the balance of power in the Senate are a message Daines contended the GOP wasn't pushing enough. "I mentioned that to the White House. And it's — that's not a silver bullet, it's a silver buckshot," of several issues Republicans should be talking about, Daines said. If Trump doesn’t have a GOP majority in the upper chamber, he said, "if we have a vacancy, Sotomayor, Clarence Thomas, who knows — we could not, President Trump could not move through a Supreme Court justice." DEMS HAND GOP FRESH MIDTERM WEAPON BY OPPOSING WIDELY USED VOTER ID The high court is aging, with conservative stalwarts on the bench, Supreme Court Justices Clarence Thomas, 78, and Samuel Alito, 76, nearing octogenarian status. Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor, 72, and Chief Justice John Roberts, 71, aren’t that far behind. "The Supreme Court as we know it would cease to exist under Troy Jackson, Abdul El-Sayed and James Talarico, who are hell-bent on replacing it with a bloated, lawless body designed to advance Democrats’ socialist agenda," NRSC spokeswoman Bernadette Breslin told Fox News Digital. Speculation has swirled over Alito after NPR earlier this year published a report declaring his retirement before swiftly retracting it. Alito added some fuel to that fire, however, during an interview with CBS earlier this month. When asked if he was considering retirement, he admitted to considering it earlier this year, and noted that "it's something I think that somebody at my age has to think about every term." DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING. HERE ARE 3 FORCES THAT COULD STOP IT Democrats haven’t been keen to support several of Trump’s nominees for a variety of positions throughout the government over the last two years. Notably, Republicans went nuclear last year to change the Senate’s rules to move through bundles of nominees that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Democrats were blocking. And Schumer suggested that a Supreme Court pick, should there be a vacancy, and other positions in the judiciary may suffer the same fate. "The bottom line is one of the reasons that we want to make sure we do everything we can to take back the Senate is not let Trump put such horrible justices, MAGA justices on the Supreme Court and the lower courts," Schumer said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Daines noted that sometimes voters look for a shortcut to head to the polls, and that the Supreme Court being a quiet issue on the ballot could very well be that path to energizing a Republican base to getting out and voting as the midterm cycle winds down. "Without a Republican majority, President Trump will not be able to move his Supreme Court nominee through, and that's a nominee that'll be on the bench for 25 years," Daines said. "We need Republicans to connect those dots. Disgruntled Republicans in Texas, come home and vote for Ken Paxton, because the Supreme Court's on the ballot."

articles.title: Biden-era FBI’s ‘Nixonian’ Trump family surveillance draws scrutiny from unlikely corner
articles.summary: Julian Epstein, a former top Democratic official, compared the FBI's tracking of Melania Trump, Barron Trump and Susie Wiles to Nixonian tactics.
articles.body: Revelations that the Biden-era FBI tracked Trump family travel and top aide Susie Wiles’ phone records received a blistering rebuke from a former top Democratic official who compared the behavior to Nixon-era abuses of federal power that surfaced amid the Watergate scandal. The FBI investigation codenamed "Plasmic Echo," later taken over by special counsel Jack Smith, examined Trump’s alleged improper retention of classified and national-defense material and possible obstruction. Records show agents tracked first lady Melania Trump's and Barron Trump’s travel while planning the 2022 Mar-a-Lago search and later logged metadata from now-Chief of Staff Susie Wiles’ calls with attorneys, journalists and others." Julian Epstein, the former chief counsel for the House Judiciary Committee’s Democratic bench, compared the situation to the scandal that brought down President Richard Nixon. JACK SMITH'S PROBE SWEPT UP FOX NEWS, OTHER MEDIA COMMUNICATIONS WITH GOVERNMENT SOURCES "It’s hard to think of good justifications for this. To me, it feels a little Nixonian," said Epstein, who also served as staff director to Democrats on a second powerful panel, the House Oversight Committee. "If this report is true, then it's pretty bad. If true, then those in charge at the time better have some darn good explanations for surveillance of family members and advisors talking privately to lawyers or exercising their free-speech rights with the news media," he said. Nixon, a California Republican, maintained an "Enemies List" developed by White House aides around top adviser Charles Colson and later formalized by White House counsel John Dean. Dean – now a vocal critic of Republicans like Trump – once described it in a 1971 memo as intended to "use the available federal machinery to screw our political enemies." Epstein questioned what legal justification investigators had for monitoring the contacts, particularly those involving lawyers and journalists. VETERAN DEM BREAKS PARTY LINE AS JACK SMITH SPYING SCANDAL GRIPS CAPITOL HILL "[That] seems like a stretch," he said. Epstein appeared to be among the few prominent Democrats publicly criticizing the newly disclosed investigative tactics Tuesday, including the tracking of Melania and Barron Trump’s travel and the collection of Wiles’ call metadata. SECRET PHONE-RECORD SEIZURE SPARKS PERSONAL LAWSUIT FROM GOP SENATOR Fox News Digital reached out to Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat who just months ago similarly broke party-silence to object to prior revelations from Smith’s probe. Blumenthal told Fox News Digital in July that Republicans were right to be upset that some of their communications were subpoenaed without their notice. "I think we need to have more facts. Look into it. Republicans are rightly concerned about the possible breach of norms and improper access to email," Blumenthal said at the time. In a separate disclosure on July 14, the GOP-led Senate Judiciary Committee released records showing that Smith’s 2020-election investigation obtained and reviewed text messages exchanged between Trump White House officials and 44 current and former members of Congress, including Republicans and Democrats. Theo Wold, a former acting assistant U.S. attorney general under Trump who later served as Idaho’s solicitor general, said the new disclosures involving Melania, Barron and Wiles vindicate Republicans who have long warned of a so-called "Deep State." "But now we know that DOJ, the FBI, and the wider intelligence community have targeted Catholics, homeschool families, pro-life prayer warriors, and even the then-leading Republican Presidential candidate and his family," Wold said. "The Deep State is real. They have abused their authority for political gain. They have wielded government power against innocent Americans to coordinate their attack on opposition political figures and dissident movements." The White House also condemned the newly disclosed tracking of Trump family travel and collection of Wiles’ call metadata. "Jack Smith’s surveillance operation was a disgraceful abuse of government power. Spying on political opponents is weaponization of law enforcement, plain and simple," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital. "Those responsible must be held accountable." On one day in March 2023, documents showed investigators logged metadata for 39 calls made or received by Wiles. Calls to and from multiple campaign contacts, a lawyer and an extension associated with Melania Trump were among those logged in Wiles’ phone metadata. Her story should inspire young women. Instead, hatred from President Trump’s opponents teaches young people that if you work for the ‘wrong’ candidate, you and those around you can become targets," Pipko told Fox News Digital. articles.title: Biden conspicuously absent from campaign trail as Obama, Harris step up for midterm push
articles.summary: Joe Biden's limited campaign trail presence contrasts sharply with Barack Obama and Kamala Harris as Democrats fight for midterm majorities.
articles.body: Former President Joe Biden has been largely absent from the campaign trail as Democrats fight to win back House and Senate majorities in November, even as former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris step up efforts to boost the party’s candidates. Biden, 83, has kept a limited public schedule while battling advanced, metastatic prostate cancer. He has endorsed candidates and is helping Democrats raise money, according to a source in Biden's political circle. But the former president has made few political appearances this year. The contrast is increasingly visible with four weeks to go until Election Day. Obama is cutting ads for Senate and gubernatorial candidates, helping the party fundraise and preparing to hit the trail during the closing stretch of the midterm campaign. Harris, the Democrats' 2024 presidential nominee, is also campaigning across key battleground states, including a recent stop in Michigan with Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. MIDTERM MATH: THE THREE FORCES THAT COULD STOP A DEMOCRATIC BLUE WAVE Biden has appeared at just a handful of political events this year. He spoke in February at a reception honoring his 2020 South Carolina primary victory, which propelled him toward the Democratic nomination and eventually the presidency. In June, he addressed a Maryland Democratic Party event. Longtime Democratic strategist Michael Ceraso told Fox News Digital that some in the party's elite and fundraising class are concerned that "if Biden were to be pushed out there in any sort of way for virtual or in-person opportunities, he could be a liability." Veteran Democratic strategist Maria Cardona had a different take, telling Fox News Digital, "There are still a ton of Americans who love Joe Biden." Biden did weigh in on a handful of Democratic primary showdowns this cycle. The former president endorsed former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms for governor. Bottoms, who served as a senior advisor in the Biden administration, won the Georgia Democratic gubernatorial nomination. The former president also backed Dan Koh, another Biden administration veteran, who captured the Democratic nomination in Massachusetts' 6th Congressional District. HEAD HERE FOR THE LATEST FOX NEWS REPORTING ON FORMER PRESIDENT BIDEN Biden is also advocating on behalf of efforts to secure democracy. "American democracy begins and ends at the ballot box. There is no more important civic duty nor fundamental right to be defended," the former president wrote on social media last month, as he cast his ballot in his home state of Delaware's primary. "Voting defines our freedom and makes everything possible." But mostly, Biden has served as a foil for President Donald Trump, who Biden ousted from the White House in the 2020 election. Four years later, Biden ended his re-election bid after a disastrous debate performance against Trump in their 2024 rematch. Trump and fellow Republicans are repeatedly blaming Biden for high prices at the gas and diesel pumps, even though public opinion polls indicate most Americans now point fingers at Trump and his administration. Biden left the presidency with poor approval ratings, as he faced high inflation, foreign policy divides, and lingering questions about his ability to serve in office. He stood at 42% approval and 57% disapproval in January 2025, in the final Fox News poll during his White House tenure. Post-presidency, Biden held a 71% favorable rating among Democrats in a CNN poll conducted in May. But Biden's favorable rating among Democrats was 25 points lower than Obama's. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB Meanwhile, some Democrats still blame him for Trump's 2024 re-election, arguing that Biden did not get out of the race in time to allow Harris to mount a successful campaign. Ceraso, a veteran of two presidential campaigns, pointed to the 2024 election and told Fox News Digital that Biden left a "bad taste with some Democrats, especially within the party's elite and fundraising class." He added, "I do not think Biden has the same level of charisma as Vice President Harris and former President Obama, and if I'm organizing an event to get thousands of people to come out, I would not do that around Biden." Cardona, a Democratic National Committee member, said Biden's health is stifling requests for campaign trail appearances. articles.title: CIA officer arrested with gold bars admits he exposed secret intelligence source to a foreign official
articles.summary: A high-ranking CIA officer arrested after federal agents said they found more than 600 pounds of gold bars stashed in his home pleaded guilty to wire fraud under an agreement with federal prosecutors.
articles.body: ALEXANDRIA, Virginia — A high-ranking CIA officer arrested after federal agents found roughly 600 pounds of gold bars stashed in his home also disclosed details about a secret U.S. intelligence source to a foreign official, prosecutors said Tuesday during his plea hearing. David Rush, 49, admitted to one count of wire fraud under an agreement with federal prosecutors and faces up to 20 years in prison when he is sentenced Jan. 28. Justice Department officials said Rush siphoned off $194 million in government funds, using his position at the CIA to create an elaborate scheme designed to facilitate his “maximum self-enrichment at the expense of the United States.” In a plea document, Rush admitted that in late 2025 he disclosed “certain descriptive information of a U.S. government clandestine human source” that could “endanger the safety and life of the human source and the U.S. government officers working with the source,” as well as jeopardize America’s “ability to recruit human sources, who rely on the U.S. government’s assurance of absolute secrecy.” Lawyers for Rush declined to comment. Rush has been in jail since his arrest May 19, after investigators said he made up details about his education and military service record, fooling the nation’s top spy agency for years. As a top officer at the CIA’s Directorate of Science and Technology, Rush had access to the nation’s most secret programs -- and he used that to his benefit, prosecutors said. Rush worked as a liaison to the Pentagon for sensitive military programs and collaborated closely with the Defense Department’s powerful second in command, Steve Feinberg, people familiar with the work have told NBC News. The case has prompted a wave of shock and anxiety among lawmakers and within the insular spy agency. How could someone have fooled the highest levels of government for decades, and how could he have gotten through what is considered a rigorous vetting process to join the CIA? The intelligence community’s watchdog is separately investigating, according to a U.S. official and a person familiar with the probe. Until Tuesday, Rush — who was placed on leave sometime before his arrest and then fired — had only formally been charged with one count of theft of public funds, accused of falsifying his pay records. His court case was postponed for weeks as his lawyers and the government worked toward a possible plea agreement. U.S. District Judge Michael Nachmanoff approved the plea deal Tuesday. Rush acted alone, using his manufactured bona fides to create confidence in his work, court documents say. No other CIA officials, government employees or contractors were accused of crimes in the case. According to court documents, his deceptions “caused contractors and subcontractors to carry out the transactions” Rush fabricated a highly classified program to funnel tens millions of dollars for his personal purchase of luxury real estate in Florida and invented a sensitive government “activity” to acquire the gold bars. “Rush effectively acted as his own approving official, enabling him to expend substantial amounts of United States government money without meaningful scrutiny,” according to court documents. During their search of his home, investigators seized about 300 gold bars, federal officials said, along with about $2 million in U.S. currency and 35 luxury watches. Initially, investigators said it was 303 bars, but on Tuesday revised that figure to 298 bars. The gold was for what Rush claimed was an official work purpose, and he had said that they were distributed out -- the spy agency uses all sorts of unusual methods in its work. Rush, according to federal prosecutors, also fabricated a classified special access program, and told associates he needed luxury real estate in South Florida for it. He had $145 million transferred to a holding company for four luxury properties and vehicles. He lied to associates, telling them that highly-placed government officials knew about the need for the real estate and approved the transaction. Rush also spent $1.8 million of the government’s money for private charter flights, but a CIA review later found he had “no legitimate official requirement” for these flights, prosecutors said. The interstate wire fraud occurred in January — when Rush caused a government employee to send $45 million for his scheme, prosecutors said. The case also has cast a spotlight on Rush’s relationship with Feinberg, as NBC News reported. The FBI reviewed video showing Rush and Feinberg at a residence in the Washington region that is linked to the federal government, according to four people familiar with the video. Feinberg has been interviewed by the FBI, according to two people familiar with the investigation, but has not been accused of any wrongdoing, and the bureau said he is not under investigation. There’s no indication that Feinberg knew of Rush’s alleged fabrications. A Pentagon spokesman has said Feinberg and Rush were not close. CIA Director John Ratcliffe said in a statement Tuesday that the agency “immediately” referred to case to the FBI after an internal investigation identified potential crimes, and said Rush “abused his position and betrayed the public trust and should be held fully accountable for his actions.” FBI Director Kash Patel said Rush “betrayed his oath, his co-workers, and the American people” when he “defrauded the government of hundreds of millions of dollars, and then misused those funds for extravagant purchases.”

articles.title: Liberal justices look for 'escape hatch' as high-stakes climate case lands at Supreme Court, experts say
articles.summary: Ketanji Brown Jackson and Sonia Sotomayor repeatedly questioned Supreme Court jurisdiction in Suncor v. Boulder, signaling a possible off-ramp.
articles.body: Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson and Sonia Sotomayor's repeated questions concerning whether the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to hear a high-profile climate case that could expose oil companies to lawsuits across the country steered conservative lawyers to believe that the liberal justices are seeking an "off-ramp." "The fact that they kept going back to trying to create a jurisdictional problem tells me they don't feel confident that they have the votes in this space," Carrie Severino, president of JCN, a conservative judicial group, told Fox News Digital. "Jackson and Sotomayor were looking for an escape hatch." The Supreme Court began its new term Monday, hearing its first oral arguments for Suncor v. Boulder, in which they will rule on whether state tort laws can be used to seek damages from oil companies for climate change, even when the alleged harms are occurring outside the state or continent. The justices will also rule on whether the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to hear this case now, as the case is still before the Colorado Supreme Court. The case before the high court is in an unusual procedural posture, meaning the justices could resolve it without ever reaching the blockbuster state-versus-federal power fight at its center. That dispute centers on whether Colorado can use its own laws to seek damages for alleged harms caused by emissions from other states or whether it's an issue for the federal government and Congress to regulate. SUPREME COURT BEGINS NEW TERM WITH HIGH-PROFILE LOOK AT CLEAN AIR AND FEDERAL AUTHORITY "The questions by Jackson and Sotomayor trying to say it would be premature for the court to issue an opinion are simply the liberal justices trying to find an off-ramp for the case because they are afraid they will be outvoted on the main issue: does federal law such as the Clean Air Act preempt all state claims like those asserted here," Hans von Spakovsky, senior legal fellow with Advancing American Freedom, told Fox News Digital. While questioning Suncor attorney Kannon Shanmugam, Jackson suggested the dispute may have reached the Supreme Court too soon, calling it "premature from the standpoint of this court exercising its jurisdiction." She also repeatedly questioned why the court couldn't wait to hear the case, saying the court doesn't "have the whole set of facts" and that the court doesn't "really know enough to be confident" that the theories posed are applicable. "It feels to me like the defendants ... are bringing it back to federal court before the state courts have really had a chance to sort out who is the source, what is their allegation with respect to how this causation is happening," Jackson told Principal Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris, who argued in support of Suncor. Meanwhile, Sotomayor refused to drop her line of questioning on jurisdiction with Shanmugam, proposing that the Supreme Court send the case back to the Colorado Supreme Court. "If we're unsure of your characterization, because there's certainly a number of amici brief who disagree with that characterization, shouldn't we be certifying this question to the Colorado court instead of us deciding it? We have to be sure of our jurisdiction before we take it," Sotomayor said. Republican Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall told Fox News Digital it was clear that the liberal justices were trying to cast doubt on whether they have jurisdiction. SUPREME COURT CAN RESTORE SANITY AND STOP THE LEFT’S RADICAL CLIMATE AGENDA "Well, I think you saw both Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor try to find an out for this court, basically saying the court doesn't have jurisdiction at this stage of the case to be able to make a final ruling. I think that you saw the advocates on behalf of Suncor be able to distinguish that." If the Supreme Court declines to reach the federalism issue, the Colorado Supreme Court's ruling allowing Boulder's state-law claims to proceed would remain in place, leaving the broader question of how far states can use tort law to pursue climate claims against energy companies unresolved. Chief Justice John Roberts pressed Boulder attorney Kevin Russell on whether a Boulder win could trigger similar lawsuits nationwide. Russell said there are legal limits, but acknowledged to Justice Clarence Thomas that Boulder's theory could allow other fossil-fuel businesses to be sued. "The chief justice and the court do not like issuing rulings with no limiting principles, rulings that could open up unlimited litigation and claims. Kannon Shanmugam, the lawyer for Suncor, emphasized this again at the very end of the oral argument when he pointed out that there are not only 90,000 political jurisdictions that could sue, but individuals could also sue claiming damages from global warming," von Spakovsky said. "And he also pointed out something the conservative majority frowns upon: that Boulder is trying to resolve a major policy issue in the courts instead of in the legislative branches," von Spakovsky continued. SUPREME COURT KICKS OFF NEW TERM WITH FRESH QUESTIONS OVER ITS LEGITIMACY AND ITS FUTURE Supporters of Suncor say the lawsuits could "bankrupt" oil companies and cause the price for consumers to go up. "It's to basically create a carbon tax on both producers and emitters across the country, which would include, by the way, my cattlemen in Alabama producing beef for our country, those that are creating concrete to be able to build structures and be able to grow our economy," Marshall told Fox News. "They ultimately want to bankrupt that industry to have their preferred climate change policies be in play." "They're literally addressing behavior that takes place all over the world," Utah Attorney General Derek Brown told Fox News Digital. "They want to regulate not just what happens in Colorado, but what happens in my state of Utah or in Saudi Arabia. That's not the way the system works. So, really, this case comes down to one main issue and that is who gets to decide things like energy policy. And ultimately, under our system, it should be Congress." Meanwhile, Boulder alleged ExxonMobil and Suncor knew for decades about the climate risks associated with fossil fuels but misled the public about those risks. The communities estimate that taxpayers could face more than $100 million in costs to adapt to climate-related impacts, including wildfires, drought and damage to roads and other infrastructure. Former Washington Gov. Jay Inslee, a Democrat and longtime advocate for aggressive action on climate change, argued those costs are already being felt by communities across the country. "As governor, I've worked with so many families who've lost their homes," Inslee told Fox News Digital. "So many communities have essentially burned down, and they ought to be able to have a day in court to hear the evidence, to determine whether the lies of the oil and gas industry legitimately, they make it so that they're held accountable." The complaint pointed to a 1977 internal memo from ExxonMobil that circulated among the company's highest-level managers. The memo reported that "current scientific opinion overwhelmingly favors" that fossil fuels contribute to the rise in CO2 emissions. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Their own scientists knew that their product was dangerous, that it was going to cause more fires. And they knew this for decades, 1967, their own scientists told them it could be catastrophic, so they knew about it, they lied about it," Inslee said. "Now it's an American right to be in court. Nobody should bar an American from their day in court."

articles.title: Russian researcher's mystery death could be ‘far worse’ than the plague, former senior Trump official warns
articles.summary: Marshall Billingslea warns the Irkutsk researcher's death could involve antibiotic-resistant plague engineered under the Soviet bioweapons program.
articles.body: The unexplained death of a researcher at a Russian anti-plague institute has one former senior U.S. arms official warning it could be 'far worse' than the bacteria that caused the Black Death. Marshall Billingslea, who served as President Donald Trump's special presidential envoy for arms control, said a top Soviet bioweapons defector told him decades ago about secret work on antibiotic-resistant plague at the same facility where the recent plague-related death occurred. "This may not be just 'the plague.' It may be far worse," Billingslea wrote on X. He spent much of the 1990s working on proliferation and arms control issues on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee — and during that time worked with Ken Alibek, the former No. 2 official in the Soviet biological weapons program who defected to the U.S. BIOWEAPON THREAT EXPOSED AS ANTHROPIC SOUNDS ALARM ON FOREIGN ACTORS PLOTTING VIRUS EXPERIMENTS "He claimed that they had engineered a strain of plague that was antibiotic-resistant & that they had worked on plague chimeras (fusing 2 or more pathogens)," Billingslea wrote of Alibek. "He specifically called out Irkutsk for being involved in the BW program," he added. Billingslea's warning comes after a 28-year-old employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East died last week from what Russian authorities have described as pneumonia of undetermined origin. Russia has not said the woman died of plague and said testing found no microorganisms in her body linked to her work. The World Health Organization (WHO) said Tuesday that Russian officials told the agency no plague or other high-threat pathogen had been detected among her close contacts, though they are still awaiting confirmation of what caused her fatal pneumonia. DEFENSE DEPARTMENT SCIENTIST’S ACCIDENTAL DEATH RAISES QUESTIONS AS PROBE INTO MISSING SCIENTISTS GROWS About 60% of the woman's identified contacts have been tested so far, according to Russian authorities, with two cases of COVID-19 and two rhinovirus infections detected — but no other infectious disease pathogens. Still, the unexplained death at a facility that works with dangerous pathogens has drawn scrutiny from biosecurity experts — including questions about why the cause remains unknown. Kevin Esvelt, an MIT professor who studies biological security and catastrophic pandemic risks, said Russia's latest explanation suggests the researcher did not die from plague while leaving unanswered what killed her. "If we take the Russian authorities at their word, it is not plague," Esvelt wrote Tuesday. "But untargeted research-grade sequencing reliably identifies pathogens, and people seldom die of pneumonia without pathogens, let alone 28-year-olds," he added. "It would be surprising if they did not know the cause." Esvelt cautioned that more alarming explanations remain hypothetical. "The concerning possibility is still only a possibility," he wrote. The questions surrounding the death come against the backdrop of the Soviet Union's documented history of secretly developing biological weapons, including weaponized plague, and U.S. assessments that elements of that program continued after the Soviet collapse. In its 2025 arms control compliance report, the State Department assessed that Russia maintains an offensive biological warfare program in violation of the Biological Weapons Convention and that the Soviet program was "absorbed, not dismantled" after the Soviet collapse. The department said the program "has continued and evolved" under the Russian Federation and that Moscow continues activities prohibited under the convention. Russia has repeatedly denied maintaining an offensive biological weapons program. The U.S. assessment does not establish any connection between Russia's biological weapons program and the researcher's death in Irkutsk, and no such connection has been confirmed. NEW YORK DECLARES MEASLES DISASTER EMERGENCY AS CASES SURGE IN PENNSYLVANIA The Soviet program Billingslea referenced was one of the world's largest clandestine biological weapons efforts. Alibek, born Kanatjan Alibekov, rose to become the first deputy chief of Biopreparat, the ostensibly civilian network that formed a major part of the Soviet biological weapons apparatus, before defecting to the United States in 1992. After his defection, Alibek provided U.S. officials with extensive information about the scale and capabilities of the Soviet program. He described Soviet scientists working to weaponize pathogens including plague and developing strains designed to withstand antibiotics. His claims about some aspects of the Soviet program have faced scrutiny over the years, making independent documentation particularly important. But the existence and enormous scale of the Soviet biological weapons effort — conducted despite Moscow's 1975 ratification of the Biological Weapons Convention — is well established. The Irkutsk institute says it was founded in 1934 as a scientific and operational center for combating plague. Its mission later expanded to other highly dangerous diseases, including cholera and anthrax, and it describes itself today as a research and anti-epidemic facility responsible for helping protect the region from infectious disease. The Trump administration has said it is closely monitoring the situation and pressed Moscow for greater transparency about what happened. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that while travel between the U.S. and Russia remains limited, an infectious disease could quickly spread beyond Russia's borders. "If something like that gets out, it could quickly spread," Rubio said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP President Donald Trump said the U.S. would offer assistance to Russia if needed. "I hate to see them having it," Trump told reporters Monday. "It's a rough disease."

articles.title: FBI says contractor failure led to hack of its jobs website
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — The FBI’s internal review of a hack of its jobs portal last month has so far determined that a “security failure” by a contractor managing the site caused the breach.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The FBI’s internal review of a hack of its jobs portal last month has so far determined that a “security failure” by a contractor managing the site caused the breach. “To date, our review has determined that the incident occurred as the result of a security failure of a platform managed by a third-party organization — after a contractor failed to implement a security patch explicitly issued to secure the platform,” Cyber Division Assistant Director Brett Leatherman said in a statement Tuesday. The statement said the FBI has removed the contractor, which it did not identify, “and taken all necessary steps to both mitigate any further risk and protect our workforce. We will continue to bring the responsible parties to justice, with multiple arrests already occurring.” The hack of the FBIJobs.gov portal took place late last month, and ShinyHunters, a cyber-extortion outfit, claimed credit for it. A representative of the group told NBC News at the time that it used the job portal to gain access to other agency programs, stealing between 2 and 3 terabytes of files. NBC News was not able to verify the extent of the claims. Leatherman’s statement appeared to confirm that the agency believes ShinyHunters is responsible. “The FBI will aggressively investigate this cyber incident involving FBIjobs.gov and the cyber-criminal group ShinyHunters with all available resources,” his statement said. FBI Director Kash Patel announced on social media last week that a member of the group had been arrested. The arrest took place on Sept. 15, a week before ShinyHunters claimed credit for the attack. “This morning @FBI and our partners the Dutch National Police are announcing the arrest of one of the alleged leaders of ShinyHunters — a global cybercrime and threat actor group linked to cyberattacks in the United States, the Netherlands, and around the world,” he wrote. “As we speak FBI teams are actively working with partners to obtain and execute more leads in the ongoing investigation based on this arrest,” his post on X said. Some FBI employees were upset to have learned about the hack from the media and said the agency had been slow to respond, a person familiar with the agency’s communications said last week. The FBI had said in a previous statement that is “in regular communication with anyone who may be impacted,” and that the agency “treats the security of its information and the safety of its workforce as top priorities.” ShinyHunters is a loosely defined group, with members scattered around the globe. It routinely hacks companies to steal their data and threatens to publish it on the dark web if not paid.

articles.title: Macron trashes American free speech as riots grip France — internet unloads: ‘Enormous fool’
articles.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron called American free speech "the opposite of free speech" as student protests and school fires sweep across France.
articles.body: French President Emmanuel Macron is drawing fierce online backlash after criticizing the American conception of free speech and arguing that liberty requires a "common framework" — remarks landing as his government faces mounting pressure from nationwide student protests, school blockades and clashes with riot police across France. "The so-called American ‘free speech’ today, which some people have promoted, is the opposite of free speech," Macron said at Complutense University in Madrid during a discussion on democracy, youth and the digital age on Sept. 29, according to a translation of his remarks. Macron argued that free speech is not absolute and must be bounded by the rights of others and respect for public order, while also arguing that the flow of information must maintain a relationship to truth. He compared those limits to restrictions against assaulting or insulting others or destroying public property. FRANCE’S TEEN RIOTS TAKE EXPLOSIVE NEW TURN AS GOVERNMENT POINTS FINGER AT HARD LEFT "There is no freedom if there is no limit to my freedom, which begins with the freedom of others and respect for a common framework. I know this when I walk down the street: my freedom cannot mean hitting you, insulting you or trashing the public space we all share," Macron added, according to a translation to English. The remarks quickly drew backlash online, with critics seizing on the contrast between Macron’s comments on free speech and the unrest unfolding at home, where protests, blockades and clashes with police are testing his government. FRANCE ROCKED BY STUDENT RIOTS AS HUNDREDS ARRESTED, VIOLENCE SPREADS NATIONWIDE "These people are going to cling to power even if it means burning their countries to the ground," said Federalist senior editor John Daniel Davidson. "Offended by the First Amendment while completely ignoring the fact his own country is literally burning to the ground," wrote one person. "His country is being destroyed by riots. Does he consider that free speech," asked another person. "Emmanuel Macron is an enormous fool," said Wikipedia co-founder Larry Sanger. "Europeans are so stupid about speech," said one user. "At this point, bringing back the Bourbons would be more dignified for France," wrote Republican Utah Sen. Mike Lee’s communication director Billy Gribbin. "The worst president France has ever had, verging on treasonous given his attempts to shut down the nation's remarkable nuclear industry and expertise," wrote Institute of Public Affairs senior fellow Adam Creighton. "We are still free in America and @EmmanuelMacron can pound sand," wrote Dan Gainor. FRANCE’S VIOLENT STUDENT PROTESTS RAISE WARNING FOR AMERICA: ‘A CAUTIONARY TALE’ Macron has previously taken aim at the American conception of free speech, declaring that "free speech is pure bulls—" if people do not know how algorithms are guiding what they see online, while calling for greater transparency and "a sort of public order" to curb racist and hate speech during a Feb. 18, appearance in New Delhi, India. Protests erupted in the Paris suburbs in mid-September over teacher shortages and school resources before rapidly spreading nationwide. Demonstrators have set fires, damaged buildings and clashed with police while France’s Education Ministry said classes were fully or partially suspended at 891 schools Tuesday, while 24 schools have been burned or ransacked since the protests began, according to the Associated Press. articles.title: ‘Medically unprecedented’: Christa Pike alive, speaking days after failed execution
articles.summary: Christa Pike is alive and speaking nearly a week after she was given to two lethal injection doses during a failed execution attempt, her attorneys confirmed Tuesday.
articles.body:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. ( WKRN ) — Christa Pike is alive and speaking nearly a week after she was given two lethal injection doses during a failed execution attempt, her attorneys confirmed Tuesday.

On Wednesday, Sept. 30, Pike received two doses of the state’s lethal injection drug pentobarbital and survived. She was taken away from Riverbend Maximum Security Prison in an ambulance to a Nashville area hospital.

Earlier this week, Pike remained incapacitated on a ventilator while medical staff worked to clear the drug from her system. However, by Tuesday, Pike’s attorneys said she was conscious, speaking and receiving critical medical care.

“We are incredibly grateful to the first responders and the medical team at the hospital who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her,” her legal team expressed. “We also want to thank thousands from all over the world who sent messages offering prayers and support for Christa.”

Pike’s attorney’s noted that she sustained “severe damage” to her arms and remains handcuffed and shackled to a hospital bed. Although her prognosis remains unclear, Pike’s legal team said, at minimum, they expect a “long recovery.”

According to officials, Pike is the only person known to have survived a complete execution attempt in the United States. Following the failed execution, Pike’s attorneys are asking Gov. Bill Lee to commute her sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.

Pike’s legal team is due in court Wednesday, Oct. 7. No additional details were immediatlely released.

articles.summary: {beacon} Energy & Environment Energy & Environment The Big Story Trump seeks to make more diesel available President Trump on Monday night moved to make more diesel available in a bid to lower fuel prices. © AP Photo/Nick Ingram “I’m going to sign a historic executive order to officially waive the off-road requirement and…
articles.body:
Trump seeks to make more diesel available

President Trump on Monday night moved to make more diesel available in a bid to lower fuel prices .

“I’m going to sign a historic executive order to officially waive the off-road requirement and allow anyone to purchase tax-free red dyed diesel for any reason,” Trump said before calling on aide Natalie Harp to bring the order on stage for him to sign.

This diesel simply has dye added to it to signal that it is tax exempt and is typically used in machines such as farm and construction equipment.

Trump signed the order at a rally for Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts (R) and Gov. Jim Pillen (R). Ricketts’ reelection bid in particular has become increasingly competitive in recent weeks.

“So Pete and Jim, this should absolutely assure your election,” the president said.

The executive order directs the Treasury Secretary to consider deferring payments of federal excise taxes for on-road uses of dyed diesel for the rest of the year.

The moves come as diesel prices have reached record highs in recent weeks and put a strain on industries that use the fuel, including agriculture and trucking. As of Monday, diesel averaged about $6.32 per gallon , according to AAA .

Tom Kloza, chief oil analyst at Gulf Oil, told The Hill that he doesn’t expect that increasing availability of red-dyed diesel will make a significant difference in the price overall.

“This is really a cosmetic gesture,” Kloza told The Hill ahead of the actual announcement based on reports that such a move was forthcoming. “This really is a Band-Aid where a tourniquet would be more appropriate.”

articles.title: Trump admin revamps price transparency
articles.summary: Click in for more news from The Hill {beacon} Healthcare Healthcare The Big Story HHS revamps price transparency rules The Trump administration is revamping its transparency rules, trying to make health insurers clearly publish the prices they negotiate with doctors and hospitals. © iStock The rule finalized by the Department of Health and Human…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is revamping its transparency rules, trying to make health insurers clearly publish the prices they negotiate with doctors and hospitals.

The rule finalized by the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), the Employee Benefits Security Administration and the IRS on Monday builds on an earlier requirement that hospitals publish their prices in a “machine-readable file” so patients can find and compare the cost of services beforehand.

Insurers and most employer-sponsored health plans currently post monthly files, listing in-network rates, out-of-network payments and drug prices.

But in practice, that information is presented in gargantuan raw data dumps that are cluttered and filled with prices for unrealistic services, like the price for a heart surgery done by a psychiatrist, or a baby delivery performed by a podiatrist.

“Simply put, you basically need a supercomputer to process the data, which has limited who can work with the data,” said Peter Nelson, who directs the Center for Consumer Information and Insurance Oversight (CCIIO) at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.

The new rules seek to make the data more standardized and usable.

It also requires insurers to report in-network rates as a dollar figure, instead of a percentage or some other estimate, though there are exceptions.

HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said the new rules would reduce file sizes of pricing data by 70 percent.

“The results will be better information for the people who need it. Patients will be better able to compare what care costs before they receive it, and lawyers will be better able to judge whether the insurers that they hire are negotiating the best prices for their workers, and researchers will be able to identify price disparities and study where the market is failing and where the system is failing,” Kennedy said.

The administration said the rule changes will save plans about $174.5 million annually.
