articles.title: Archdiocese of St. Louis sues ICE officials over blocked religious services
articles.summary: The lawsuit argues that the jail’s visitation policy prevents Catholic detainees from practicing important parts of their faith.
articles.body:
ST. LOUIS, Mo. (KTVI) — The Archdiocese of St. Louis has filed a lawsuit against Ste. Genevieve County officials and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) leadership over alleged restrictions on Catholic religious services for immigration detainees.

The federal lawsuit, filed Monday, claims that the Ste. Genevieve County Jail and ICE have violated the First Amendment rights of immigrant detainees by preventing Catholic priests from delivering communion, hearing confessions and celebrating Mass.

The lawsuit argues that the jail’s visitation policy prevents Catholic detainees from practicing important parts of their faith.

According to the lawsuit, Catholic priests are required to have in private, face-to-face contact with detainees to fulfill certain religious obligations for confession and communion. The lawsuit claims, however, that current jail policies make that impossible because visits must take place through glass barriers using a telephone system with no physical contact.

The Ste. Genevieve County Jail’s website states that jail visitations are limited to a single four-hour window on Sundays with 30-minute visitation blocks available on a first-come, first-serve basis.

According to the lawsuit, some attorneys and consular officials are granted exceptions to both the no-contact and time-limitation policies. The Archdiocese argues that this amounts to unequal treatment because comparable religious and secular activities could be offered with those visitations.

The Archdiocese says it has repeatedly made requests for face-to-face visits for the administration of Catholic sacraments, but those requests have been denied.

According to the lawsuit, Andrew Johnson, the jail administrator in Ste. Genevieve County, told the Archdiocese that such visits were not possible because of the facility’s no-contact visitation policy, adding that “the visitation policy was implemented by ICE” and that he had no authority to change it.

The lawsuit alleges that the jail houses immigrant detainees through agreements with ICE and receives federal funding for those detainees. It argues that, as a result, ICE officials have the authority to ensure that appropriate religious accommodations are provided.

The lawsuit asks the court to declare the Ste. Genevieve County Jail’s visitation policies as unconstitutional and for an order to prohibit county officials from enforcing them. It also seeks an order preventing ICE from sending federal funds and additional immigration detainees to the facility until accommodations are made for Catholic religious services and sacraments.

Nexstar’s KTVI has reached out to officials with the St. Genevieve County Jail and ICE on the lawsuit. A Ste. Genevieve County Jail spokesperson told KTVI the jail has not yet received documentation of the lawsuit, but once that happens, it will be forwarded to legal counsel for review. ICE has not yet returned our request for comment.

The lawsuit lists Sheriff Gary Stolzer, Chief Deputy Jason Schott and Lt. Andrew Johnson from Ste. Genevieve County, along with U.S. Department of Homeland Security Director Markwayne Mullin and acting ICE Director David J. Venturella.

articles.title: Trump says Reflecting Pool repairs are near complete, refill to come ‘this week’
articles.summary: President Trump said Tuesday repairs to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool are close to complete and should be refilled with water “this week,” but still touted unfounded claims of vandalism. “I think they’re going to fill it up this week,” Trump said in a video shared by the Rapid Respond 47 account on the social…
articles.body:
President Trump said Tuesday repairs to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool are close to complete and should be refilled with water “this week,” but still touted unfounded claims of vandalism.

“I think they’re going to fill it up this week,” Trump said in a video shared by the Rapid Respond 47 account on the social platform X, featuring the president talking to reporters outside the White House.

“The Reflecting Pool is totally complete, and we changed the old pipes we wanted to get open for July 4,” he said, later adding that “I think it’s almost complete, from what I understand.”

Trump also said new grass was installed in the grounds between the Reflecting Pool and the National World War II Memorial after it was “destroyed with the letters, the famous letters.” Etched in the grass were the numbers “86 47,” a sign of opposition to Trump, but the administration has insisted it was a call for political violence against the president.

“And that’s been just about completed,” Trump added.

The president also suggested that the issues with the pool since earlier this year were caused by vandals, though a recent filing from U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro cast doubt on that narrative and instead blamed botched work.

“Well, we had vandalism there and we have it about as vandal-proof as you can get. But only sick people do that, and we have their pictures.”

Trump previously suggested late in August that the pool would “be opening in a few weeks. Will be a beauty. NO VANDALS PLEASE.” Weeks earlier, however, he claimed that there was “ some contractor error ” with the renovations that left part of the pool with “relatively inconsequential” damage.

The Reflecting Pool has been a source of controversy since the spring, when the president touted a multimillion-dollar project to restore it and coat the bottom with “American flag blue” paint. The work was done with no-bid contracts, a particular point of scrutiny.

The paint appeared to float to the pool’s surface in clumps after it was refilled, as the water appeared green due to algae blooms.

Trump, Pirro and the Interior Department said vandalism caused the damage, though Trump and Pirro have pointed toward the restoration being botched after charges were dropped for several people accused of vandalizing the Reflecting Pool.

One of those charged was former U.S. Olympian canoeist David Hearn, whose attorneys on Tuesday asked Department of Justice (DOJ) and Interior Department watchdogs to look into what they describe as a flawed investigation and prosecution.

D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman permanently dismissed the DOJ’s case, calling it a “lightning-fast indictment process,” and barred officials from charging Hearn again in the future. He suggested that Pirro’s office could resurrect the case if Trump possibly applied “political pressure” to prosecute anyone suspected of being vandals.

articles.title: Planned Parenthood Votes adds $1M to ad campaigns in Maine, Michigan
articles.summary: Planned Parenthood is investing an additional $1 million in ad buys to boost Democratic Senate candidates in Maine and Michigan. The latest investment in the states by Planned Parenthood Votes — a super PAC affiliated with Planned Parenthood — will fund digital ad campaigns targeting Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.).…
articles.body:
Planned Parenthood is investing an additional $1 million in ad buys to boost Democratic Senate candidates in Maine and Michigan.

The latest investment in the states by Planned Parenthood Votes — a super PAC affiliated with Planned Parenthood — will fund digital ad campaigns targeting Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.).

Collins is seeking a sixth term in the upper chamber against former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson (D), while Rogers is taking on former Wayne County health official Abdul El-Sayed (D) in the race to succeed outgoing Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.).

Planned Parenthood Votes’ $1 million investment beefs up its spending in the two Senate races, as the super PAC has already spent $600,000 and $800,000 on ads in Maine and Michigan, respectively.

Planned Parenthood Votes unveiled its $47 million “We Decide” ad campaign over the summer, intended to unseat lawmakers whom the super PAC claim voted to defund Planned Parenthood — which provides reproductive healthcare, including abortion procedures.

Collins and GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), though, sided with Democrats last year in striking a provision from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that proposed barring Planned Parenthood health centers from receiving Medicaid funding for services provided to low-income women.

Jackson, the Democrat opposing Collins in Maine, was also previously opposed to abortion before pivoting during his time in the state Senate.

“I’ve made mistakes early on in understanding” abortion, Jackson told The New York Times in July. “Regardless of this U.S. Senate race, I’m really, really proud of how I’ve turned that around and … done the right thing. I mean, I was wrong.”

Jackson has also criticized Collins for voting to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh in 2018.

Kavanaugh was part of the majority in the high court’s 2022 ruling in Dobbs vs. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which overturned Roe vs. Wade and struck down the federal right to an abortion.

Sarah Standiford, the executive director of Planned Parenthood Votes, said in a Tuesday release that Collins and Rogers “can’t be trusted to protect our rights or our healthcare.”

Sandiford added, “It’s our job to make sure every voter knows that before they cast their ballot. Our message is resonating online and at the doors, and moving voters, so we’re putting more resources behind it in two races where we know Planned Parenthood Votes can make a big difference.”
